body_markdown:
For almost 30 years, Bonhams held its Monterey Car Week auction at Quail Lodge, and in that time it moved some of the most expensive cars the auction house (or anyone) has ever sold, including a Ferrari 250 GTO ($38M in 2014) and a 412P ($30M in 2023). Broad Arrow snagged a spot at the Quail in 2026, however, so Bonhams put together an auction at Laguna Seca Raceway, home of the Rolex Monterey Motorsports Reunion.


Other sales have come and gone from Monterey over the years. Bonhams commendably persisted but is now the smallest auction of the week by both car count and sales totals, and that was especially clear this year with just 56 vehicles on offer. Some were race cars in keeping with the venue and the sounds of vintage racing in the background, but mostly the run list was the typical mix of interesting prewar stuff, 1950s and ’60s sports cars, and modern exotics.


We were on the ground in Monterey and looked over the most important cars crossing the block during the course of the week. Here, we examine some of the favorites from Bonhams.


## Lot 47: 1963 Meyers Manx Dune Buggy


Greg Ingold


**Sold for $42,560**


*Chassis no. 4884938. Metallic green over white vinyl. Modified restoration, #2 condition.*


**Equipment:** 1776cc/80hp VW flat-four, four-speed, Baja Pro tires, hub caps, drum brakes, teakwood rear deck, lowered stance from stock.


**Condition:** Offered by the Meyers Manx Heritage Collection. Very good condition throughout, though there are some small dings to the floor pan on the right side and the header pipe paint has wear.


**Bottom line:** Built (in kit form) on the cheap and plentiful[Beetle](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/volkswagen/beetle/1966/1966-volkswagen-beetle-base?id=aCn1I000000DDEPSA4) platform and designed by Californian Bruce Meyers, the original Meyers Manx popularized the dune buggy concept in this country and is such a fixture of American automotive culture that the original prototype was inducted into the National Historic Vehicle Register in 2024. Clean original examples are scarce and have been trading hands at substantial prices for a few years now. So although nearly 43 grand for a Beetle-based kit car seems steep, it’s on the low end of recent sales. The Meyers Manx has also been resurrected as an EV, and a new one *starts* at 75 grand, so this green one doesn’t seem like a bad value at all.


## Lot 48: 1995 Mercedes-Benz E60 AMG Limited


Greg Ingold


**Sold for $313,000**


*Chassis no. WDB1240361C17971. Brilliant Silver Metallic over black leather with gray airbrushed inserts. Unrestored original, #3+ condition.*


**Equipment:** 5956cc/381hp V-8, automatic, sunroof, cassette player, AMG Aero III wheels, Michelin Pilot Sport tires.


**Condition:** One of 62 E60 AMGs completed and just one of two finished at AMG Japan. Came to the U.S. late last year. Recently recommissioned by marque specialists. Good, original paint, with only a handful of chips and scrapes to the lower bumper. The underbody and the engine show mild use and deterioration of finishes. The seats show some cracks and creases to the leather, but otherwise the interior presents well, and the airbrushed seats are awesome. Showing 47,962 km (29,802 miles). Overall, an attractive and original pre-merger AMG.


Bonhams


Bonhams


**Bottom line:** Based on the Mercedes-Benz W124 chassis, the Porsche-built E500 is already a sought-after highway weapon, but the “E60” made things even better with input from AMG, then still an independent tuning house. The main upgrades from the firm were the hand-built 5.95-liter M119 V-8, AMG-specific suspension and exhaust, AMG wheels, and body kit. Interest in pre-merger AMGs has continued to grow as collectors recognized the workmanship that went into their builds, as well as just how scarces some of the models are. An E60 coming to market is a rare opportunity, and this one got a lot of attention. For reference, even the cleanest E500s in the world don’t stretch much past $100K in the current market.


## Lot 39: 1961 Aston Martin DB4 Series III Coupe


Greg Ingold


**Sold for $190,400**


*Chassis no. DB4619R. Black over black leather. Visually maintained, largely original, #4+ condition.*


**Equipment:** RHD. 3670cc/240hp, four-speed, wire wheels, Motorola radio, woodrim steering wheel, dash clock.


**Condition:** Known history from new and single-family ownership from 1969 to 2019. Believed original paint is dull and deteriorated. There is flaking behind the right rear wheel, burn-through on the roof and deck lid, and chips throughout the finish. The interior is heavily worn. Aged, but original.


**Bottom line:** A non-Vantage, right-hand drive coupe is the most affordable way to get into a[DB4](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/search?q=aston+martin+db4) , and prices for many vintage Astons have been trending downward in recent years. For example, Bonhams sold this car in 2019 for £287,500 (about $365,700), and it was a $169,500 no-sale on Bring a Trailer in March of this year before selling at no reserve here for $190,400. It’s a very low result for a mostly sound car, but the cost to restore, paint, and retrim this DB4 would be more expensive than it’s ever been, and the bidders probably took that into account before raising their paddles.


## Lot 24: 1967 Vollstedt-Ford 67 Indy Car


Bonhams


**Sold for $698,000**


*Chassis no. 67B. Yellow with black seat. Older restoration, #3 condition.*


**Equipment:** 255cid/500hp DOHC Ford V-8 with mechanical fuel injection, Hewland four-speed.


**Condition:** Competition history with Jim Clark, Chris Amon, Cale Yarborough, Gordon Johncock, Tom Sneva, and George Follmer behind the wheel. Extensive, known history with more than 30 races in three years in period. Qualified for the Indy 500 three times. Later restored and shown at the 2018 Pebble Beach Concours, and it won its class at the 2020 Amelia Island Concours. Good older paint overall with one notable crack to the engine cover. Mechanicals are in good condition but not overdone, and the interior shows some aging, though not excessive.


**Bottom line:** The market for vintage Indy cars isn’t huge relative to equivalent Grand Prix machinery, since both the international appeal and opportunities for use are more limited. And though Rolla Vollstedt was a prominent Indy car builder and the first to bring a rear-engined Offenhauser car to Indy, a Vollstedt never won the 500 and is far from a household name. That said, the absolutely stacked roster of drivers and extensive period history pushed the car to a strong result. Bonhams also offered an ex-Dan Gurney Lola T70 Can-Am car at Laguna Seca this year but it was a no-sale at a $900K bid, making the yellow Indy car the most significant race car to change hands at this sale.


## Lot 43: 1916 Rauch & Lang BX6 Brougham


Greg Ingold


**Sold for $84,000**


*Chassis no. 31533. Black over gray cloth. Unrestored original, #4 condition.*


**Equipment:** 80-volt electric motor, tiller steering, pop-out windshield, Waltham dash clock.


**Condition:** Built by Cleveland-based Rauch & Lang Carriage Company, which started making electrics of its own design in 1905. In a family collection and museum for 75 years. Upgraded with modern batteries and new tires. Original condition throughout, with faded, chipped paint and lackluster brightwork. The interior shows dulling but the upholstery is not torn or damaged. A magnificently original EV that reportedly cost eight times more than a Ford Model T when it was new, and is now 110 years old.


Bonhams


**Bottom line:** Given the growing relevance of electric cars in our world today, it makes sense that collectors are looking back to the electrics of the early 20th century in a new light. This one’s level of preservation, combined with its updated drivetrain for usability, make it uniquely appealing, and the bidders rewarded it, though the final price falls short of Bonhams’ $100K low estimate.


## Lot 54: 1960 Flying Caduceus Jet-Powered Land Speed Record Car


Greg Ingold


**Sold for $67,200**


*Chassis no. 1525. Red and black. Unrestored original, #3- condition.*


**Equipment:** 6930hp General Electric J-47-19 Turbojet jet engine, 14-inch Halibrand disc brakes, eight-foot ribbon parachute, 34-inch aluminum wheels, 48-inch diameter tires. Comes with a display engine.


**Condition:** Home-built and with tire support from Firestone. The first pure jet-powered land speed car. Went to Bonneville in 1962 and ’63 and clocked 359.7 mph but never broke the land speed record. Old paint with deterioration at the edges of the panels. Original interior.


**Bottom line:** This jet-powered car has serious presence with its massive size and jet fighter appearance. It’s also fairly significant, as it preceded all the other jet-powered Bonneville cars, including the current land speed record holder. But that’s really all it has going for it. It’s not in running condition, and there are far more economical ways to go fast at Bonneville. Its likely destiny is as a garage piece with some interesting history, so the price here seems reasonable.


## Lot 52: 2000 Lamborghini Diablo GT


Greg Ingold


**Sold for $2,425,000**


*Chassis no. ZA9DE21A0YLA12561. Black Rage over Nero leather. Original, #2- condition.*


**Equipment:** 5992cc/575hp V-12, five-speed, OEM Lamborghini briefcase.


**Condition:** Number 74 of 80 produced. U.S. ownership since 2007. Good older paint without major flaws to the finish, but the interior shows plenty of wear with creases to the seats and bubbling to the dash pad. Older, original car in moderately used condition. Showing 14,208 km (8828 miles).


**Bottom line:** With revised aero, a wider track, lighter weight, and more power, the[Diablo GT](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/lamborghini/diablo/1999/1999-lamborghini-diablo-gt?id=aCn1I000000DDPkSAO) represented a limited-build, high-performance package introduced just before the model ceased production. That’s a recipe for collectibility, and that was the case here. We rarely see them come up for sale, but this is the new record for a Diablo of any kind at auction—49% higher than the previous record of[$1,627,500](https://rmsothebys.com/auctions/mi26/lots/r0092-1994-lamborghini-diablo-se30/) for a 1-of-150 SE30 model set in March of this year.


## Lot 45: 2024 Bugatti Chiron Super Sport


Greg Ingold


**Sold for $4,570,000**


*Chassis no. VF9SW3V39RM795109. Glacier with Rouge Étoilé accents over Italian Red and Blanc leather. Original, #2 condition.*


**Equipment:** 7993cc/1600hp quad-turbo W-16, automatic, red calipers, Sky View roof, red seatbelts, dancing elephant logos on the seat headrests finished in gold stitching.


**Condition:** One of 80 produced and offered from the original owner. Singular Sur Mesure (custom tailored) commission with a represented $450,000 in custom options. Represented with 1325 miles and in like-new condition inside and out with no real indication of use.


**Bottom line:** Although Bugatti only built around 500 Chirons in total, there were numerous special versions. The Super Sport model is a development of the 300+, which has a claimed top speed of 300 mph. The Super Sport, meanwhile, is “limited” to 273, but it doesn’t look like anyone has maxed out the needle on this one. A $4.57M price probably isn’t far off from what it cost new given all the options, and it was Bonhams’ most expensive car in Monterey this year by nearly a factor of two.
